title: Clean chord changes: G to C
summary: Switch between G and C on guitar without buzzing or stopping, at a steady slow tempo.
learningObjectives: Move between G and C using the shortest finger path
Keep a steady beat while changing
keyTakeaways: Practise the change, not the chords
Slow and clean beats fast and sloppy
Short daily sessions beat one long one
explanation:
A chord change is the hardest part of beginner guitar. The trick is to practise **the movement between two chords**, not each chord alone.

Good looks like this: your fingers land together, every string rings, and you do not stop the beat. Do this drill **once a day for about 10 minutes**, and make the target a little harder each week.

steps.title: Set up
steps.instruction: Sit with the guitar upright and tune it. Place your fingers for G (second finger on the 6th string, 3rd fret; first finger on the 5th string, 2nd fret; third finger on the 1st string, 3rd fret).
steps.check: Strum once: all six strings ring.
steps.snag: A muted string usually means a finger is touching its neighbour; arch your fingers.

steps.title: Find the shortest path
steps.instruction: Look for a finger that barely moves between G and C. Keep your third finger as a guide and move the others around it.
steps.check: You can name which finger moves least.
steps.snag: Lifting every finger at once makes the change slow; move them together as one shape.

steps.title: Change without strumming
steps.instruction: Move from G to C and back, saying 'change' on each switch, with no strumming. Go slowly enough to land every finger.
steps.check: All fingers land at the same moment.
steps.snag: Looking away from the neck breaks your aim; look at it until it feels automatic.

steps.title: Add the beat
steps.instruction: Strum once per chord at 60 beats per minute with a metronome, switching on the beat.
steps.check: You change without stopping for 8 bars.
steps.snag: Rushing to catch up; if you fall behind, slow the metronome by 5 bpm.

blocks.title: Today's practice session

parts.label: Warm-up
parts.instruction: Stretch your fingers and play each chord once, slowly.
parts.target: Every string rings in both chords

parts.label: Main drill
parts.instruction: Change G to C and back with no strumming, then with one strum per chord at 60 bpm.

parts.label: Use it for real
parts.instruction: Play a four-bar loop (G, C, G, C) with a simple down-strum pattern.

blocks.note: Stop if your fingers or wrist hurt. Raise the tempo by 5 bpm only when the target is easy.

commonMistakes: Practising fast and building sloppy habits
Skipping the metronome, so the beat drifts
Lifting all fingers high off the strings

quiz.question: Your G to C change is buzzing and late. What is the best first fix?
options: Slow the tempo until every finger lands together
quiz.explanation: Slowing down lets the fingers learn the path; speed comes later.

quiz.question: Which part of the drill builds the movement without the strumming hand getting in the way?
quiz.explanation: Removing the strumming isolates the fretting-hand movement.

quiz.question: A muted string most often means:
options: The guitar is out of tune
A finger is touching the neighbouring string
quiz.explanation: A flat finger touching the next string stops it from ringing; arch the fingers.

socraticChallenge.scenario: You have practised G to C for two weeks and it is not getting faster.
socraticChallenge.question: What would you change about your practice?
socraticChallenge.idealAnswer: Slow down, isolate the change without strumming, check for a muted string, and shorten but repeat the sessions daily rather than practising longer less often.

exercises.prompt: Set a one-minute timer and count clean G to C changes.
exercises.answer: Success: 20 clean changes in a minute with every string ringing.

exercises.prompt: Your change is clean but you stop the beat. What is the most likely cause?
exercises.answer: You are changing too slowly for the tempo; lower the metronome until you can keep the beat, then raise it.

reviewCards.prompt: Why practise the change between two chords instead of each chord alone?
reviewCards.answer: The movement is the hard part; isolating it trains the fingers' path.

reviewCards.prompt: What should you do if you fall behind the metronome while changing chords?
reviewCards.answer: Slow the metronome by about 5 bpm and rebuild from there.
